entry.evidence: In this study, we hypothesize that the unusually large tsunami of 1662 was caused by the coseismic slipping of the focal area

sequences.source_document: Publisher XML text (jats_text) checked against the published PDF

steps.action: The authors take from historical records the 1662 tsunami heights (4–5 m at Miyazaki), about 1 m of subsidence and intensity up to 6, and note the tsunami was larger than typical M7 events.
steps.quote: The 1662 tsunami was much larger in scale than those usually generated by the repeated M7 class interplate earthquakes

steps.action: They state that earlier tsunami-deposit studies cover only the Miyazaki plain and cannot fix the inundation area.
steps.quote: these geological records are control points but are not enough to determine tsunami [...]

steps.action: They hypothesize that the 1662 tsunami came from coseismic slip of both the usual M7 interplate area and the shallow slow-earthquake source area.
steps.quote: In this study, we hypothesize that the unusually large tsunami of 1662 was caused by the coseismic slipping of the focal area

steps.action: They review earlier source estimates of the 1662 event: Hatori's near-coast tsunami source, Matsu'ura et al.'s interplate M7.2–7.5 from intensities, and Nakata et al.'s M7.6 model.
steps.quote: The earthquake was characterized as an interplate earthquake with estimated magnitude of M7.2–7.5.

steps.action: They pose the question of the rupture area and type, noting that no fault model yet satisfies both the 1 m subsidence and the 4–5 m height constraints.
steps.quote: Thus, details including the rupture area and type of the 1662 Hyuga-nada earthquake are not clear.

steps.action: From the Tohoku-oki 2011 case (Ito et al. 2013, 2017), they derive the expectation that a fault area with shallow slow slip can rupture seismically and make large tsunamis.
steps.quote: suggesting that the faults that undergo slip in slow slip events can also rupture seismically

steps.action: They design a three-subfault source model (each 80 × 25 km, strike 212°, rake 90°, dip and depth from the Nakanishi et al. plate model) that includes the shallow slow-earthquake area up-dip and a down-dip subfault for strong shaking.
steps.quote: we constructed the fault model including the parameters of the source region where there is active seismicity related to slow earthquakes

steps.action: Building on deposits reported in the Miyazaki plain, they cored and dug to 2 m at 62 lowland sites in Miyazaki and Kagoshima and found a new sandy event deposit at Komei, Nichinan City.
steps.quote: to predictively confirm 1662 deposits at 62 survey sites in the lowlands along the eastern Kyushu

steps.action: Comparing grain size, roundness and shell fragments with modern beach and river sands, they rule out a river-flood origin; citing the absence of storm deposits nearby, plus distance and elevation, they argue against a storm origin.
steps.quote: it is reasonable that event deposits were formed by a large-scale tsunami event rather than a storm

steps.action: Using a published background sedimentation rate (0.1–0.4 cm per 100 yr), they infer an age of several hundred years, correlate the deposit with 1662, and adopt it as a southern control point.
steps.quote: event deposits recognized in this study could have been formed by a tsunami approximately several hundred years ago

steps.action: They compute seafloor deformation with Okada (1985) and propagate the tsunami with linear shallow-water equations on a 3-arc-second grid and non-linear inundation equations on a 1-arc-second Komei grid (Manning 0.025, dt 0.05 s).
steps.quote: non-linear shallow water equations were solved using a finite difference scheme

steps.action: They set slips of 8, 4 and 2 m and an 80 km length as the values needed to explain the historical heights, the Komei inundation and the structural damage, giving M0 = 9.8 × 10^20 Nm (Mw 7.9).
steps.quote: a slip of 8 m at subfault 1 and a slip of 4 m at subfault 2 were needed to explain the tsunami heights

steps.action: They compare computed coastal heights with historical heights (Figure 5, p. 1904) and the computed Komei inundation with the deposit sites (Figure 6, p. 1905).
steps.quote: The computed tsunami heights along the coast of the Miyazaki plain agree with tsunami heights of 4–5 m in historical records.

steps.action: They check the 2 m down-dip slip against typical repeated M7 events (about 1 m slip, intensity 5) as a reference for the intensity-6 shaking of 1662.
steps.quote: a 2 m slip can be considered an appropriate value

steps.action: Where computed and historical heights differ, they attribute the mismatch to sea-surface versus on-land runup heights and to river runup, rather than revising the source model.
steps.quote: it is assumed that tsunami heights in historical records are high because of the effects of the runup tsunami along the river

steps.action: They check the model at Komei (flow depths of 1–4 m at all six deposit sites; no inundation at the 15 m site without deposit) and against independent deposits from previous studies in the Miyazaki plain.
steps.quote: At the highest point where event deposit was not identified by this survey, located at 15 m elevation, computed tsunami was not reached.

steps.action: They keep the claim that the Mw 7.9 model, including slip of the slow-earthquake source area, explains the deposits and historical heights, and conclude the event was possibly the largest in Hyuga-nada.
steps.quote: caused by large slip at the active source area of slow earthquakes

end.claim: A three-subfault interplate model of Mw 7.9 that includes coseismic slip of the shallow slow-earthquake source area (8 and 4 m up-dip, 2 m down-dip, 80 km long) explains the historical tsunami heights and the distribution of likely 1662 tsunami deposits at Komei and in the Miyazaki plain.

decisive_move.sentence: Setting the subfault slips and length to the values needed to reproduce the historical heights and the Komei inundation produced the Mw 7.9 model on which every comparison and the kept claim rest.

gates.evidence: The hypothesis directed the design of the fault model (§2.3 ¶1). Survey sites were chosen from prefectural inundation maps and earlier deposits (§3 ¶2), not from the hypothesis. The model could have failed to reach the deposit sites, and the 15 m no-deposit site is a real control (§6 ¶3). However, slips and length were tuned to the same Komei inundation and Miyazaki heights they are then compared with (§5 ¶1), and the interplate-only rival was never simulated. Nothing is reported as fixed before the data.

linear and non-linear shallow water equations

novelty_claims.quote: namely a subsidence of about 1 m and tsunami heights of 4–5 m at the Miyazaki plain, has not been proposed before
we newly found a sandy event deposit interbedded with silt in Komei, Nichinan City
the southern area, where there have been no reports of tsunami deposits

limits:
1. Review history: none supplied, so no review sequence is coded.

2. No sensitivity tests: there are none for slip, length, Manning coefficient, rigidity, or past versus present topography (the last is only flagged, §5 ¶2).

3. Rival not simulated: the interplate-only model was never run, so the claim that up-dip slip is needed (§2.3 ¶1) is asserted rather than shown.

4. Fit and test share data: slips and the 80 km length were chosen to fit the same Komei inundation and Miyazaki heights later used as agreement (§5 ¶1, §6 ¶3). The Komei comparison is therefore largely a fit, not a test. This is an inference from the wording 'needed to explain'.

5. Subsidence constraint not shown: the 1 m subsidence, stated as a constraint (§2.1 ¶2), is never compared with the model. The computed minimum subsidence is −0.46 m (§4 ¶1), and the paper does not say whether the Miyazaki plain value is met.

6. Deposit dating is weak: the age rests on a cited sedimentation rate, with no radiometric dating. Storm origin is excluded by analogy to neighboring sites.

7. Sub-claim statuses:
- Komei deposit as a 1662 tsunami deposit: best_explanation, tentative ('possibly').
- Mw 7.9: an estimate without stated uncertainty or resolution, so short of estimate_with_resolution.
- 'Largest Hyuga-nada earthquake': stated as possible.

8. Overstatement: the abstract's 'Hypotheses ... have been found to be correct' (§0 ¶1) goes beyond the hedged conclusion (§7 ¶1). This is an inference.

disagreements.support: The authors present a longer model with shallow slow-earthquake slip (Mw 7.9) that explains the heights and deposits, but they do not simulate the earlier models to show that those fail.
disagreements.quote: modern understanding is an improvement over the fault model of the interplate earthquake, obtained by changing the length

disagreements.target: Historical tsunami height records (Hatori 1985; Tsuji et al. 2018)
disagreements.support: Higher historical heights at some points are attributed to on-land and river runup, unlike the computed sea-surface heights; no quantitative check is given.
disagreements.quote: it is assumed that tsunami heights in historical records are high because of the effects of the runup tsunami along the river

alternatives_considered.chosen: Tsunami origin of the Komei event deposit
alternatives_considered.reason: Provenance (grain size, roundness, shell fragments unlike river sand); previous studies found no storm deposits in the Miyazaki plain; distance from the coastline and elevation

alternatives_considered.chosen: Fault model including the shallow slow-earthquake source area (up-dip subfaults 1 and 2)
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Interplate-only M7-class fault models of previous studies
alternatives_considered.reason: Recent geophysical findings and the Tohoku-oki analogy that slow-slip areas can rupture seismically
